name: IEEE PES Trending Tech: Machine Learning and Physics-Informed AI for Power Systems
title: IEEE PES Trending Tech: Machine Learning and Physics-Informed AI for Power Systems
answer: IEEE PES publishes Trending Tech pages that map machine learning research across power systems, microgrids and physics-informed methods. The most useful single point is that pure data-driven algorithms often fail at monitoring, sequential decision-making, optimisation and control, so researchers are embedding power system models into loss functions, data preprocessing and network architectures, a shift the pages document through reports, working groups and cited papers.

sections.body: These are Trending Tech pages published by the IEEE Power and Energy Society, the standards and research body for the power industry. The pages read cover physics-informed machine learning in power systems, machine learning for microgrid resiliency, stability, control and operation, and machine learning for power systems generally. Each page is a curated entry point rather than a single report, listing technical reports, papers, tutorials, workshops, panel sessions and the active committees and working groups behind them. The pages name the Working Group on Machine Learning for Power Systems under the Technologies and Innovations Subcommittee of the Power System Operation, Planning and Economics Committee, and give contact information for its chair, Fangxing Fran Li. No publication date is stated for the pages themselves, though the cited literature runs from 2014 to 2025.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The pages treat machine learning as one of the emerging technologies for implementing the next generation smart grid, with applications across generation, transmission, distribution, microgrids and customers. The physics-informed page makes the central argument: off-the-shelf supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement learning and generative models have been widely adopted by researchers, but pure data-driven algorithms often do not yield satisfactory results for power system monitoring, sequential decision-making, optimisation and control. The response has been physics-informed, physics-inspired and physics-based machine learning, combining power system models with advanced techniques. Domain knowledge embedded into algorithms includes the high or low entropy of certain sensor data, the low-rank property of streaming data matrices, physical models for generation resources, power flow models, optimality conditions, and dynamic and control models. Where a problem can be modelled as the sum of a machine learning model and a physics-based model, parameters of the two can be fitted iteratively to convergence. In the general case the physical knowledge must be embedded directly into data preprocessing, the loss function or the neural network architecture. The microgrid page adds that microgrids operate grid-connected and islanded, transitioning without interrupting supply, and that optimal operation and stable control are hard because of complex dynamics and uncertainties in inverter-based and stochastic sources. Deep reinforcement learning and imitation-based control show potential for real-time adaptive decision-making.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The physics-informed page states that by the end of last year the electric utility industry was swamped by more than two petabytes of smart meter data alone. It names the Working Group on Data-Driven Modeling, Monitoring and Control in Power Distribution Networks, and the Distribution System Operation and Planning Subcommittee. The microgrid page names the Task Force on Reinforcement Learning for Power System Dynamic Control and the Task Force on Datasets for Machine Learning of Dynamic Stability Prediction. Cited works include IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid, IEEE Transactions on Power Systems, IEEE Power and Energy Magazine and IEEE Access, with one cited paper on federated reinforcement learning for networked microgrids dated March 2025 and another on deep learning for converter-based microgrids marked early access 2025.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For a reader following AI in the energy industry, these pages are a map of where the technical community believes data-driven methods break down and what it is doing about it. The distinction between pure data-driven algorithms and physics-informed ones is the substantive point: it tells practitioners why generic machine learning tools underperform on grid monitoring, optimisation and control, and where to look for methods that respect power flow, optimality conditions and dynamic models. The pages also identify the working groups and task forces setting the research agenda, and the literature they consider foundational, which makes them useful for locating standards-adjacent work on machine learning in power systems.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Energy

sections.body: The pages are curated reading lists and programme descriptions rather than original research or standards documents. They summarise positions and cite papers but give no data of their own beyond the smart meter figure, no benchmark results and no implementation guidance. Coverage is partial, weighted toward the working groups and publications of one committee, and the cited literature is drawn from IEEE venues. The pages carry no stated publication date, so the currency of the summaries depends on when the underlying lists were last updated.
